questions.q: The element with the highest electronegativity is:
questions.solution:
**Fluorine**, at $4.0$ on the Pauling scale — the most electronegative element there is.

Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, putting fluorine at the extreme top right of the reactive elements.

questions.q: Which alkaline earth metal hydroxide is the least soluble in water?
questions.solution:
Hydroxide solubility **increases** down Group 2, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_{2}$ is the least soluble.

That is why it is safe as milk of magnesia — it dissolves too little to be caustic, but enough to neutralise stomach acid.

questions.q: The hybridisation of the central atom in $\text{SF}_{6}$ is:
questions.solution:
Six bonding pairs require six hybrid orbitals: $\mathbf{sp^{3}d^{2}}$, giving an **octahedral** shape.

Sulphur can expand its octet because it has accessible $3d$ orbitals; oxygen, in the second period, cannot — which is why $\text{OF}_{6}$ does not exist.

questions.q: Which ion is colourless in aqueous solution?
questions.solution:
$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ — a **completely filled** d sub-shell, so no d–d transition is possible and the ion is **colourless**.

The same is true of $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ($d^{0}$) at the other end of the series.

questions.q: The oxidation state of cobalt in $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_{3})_{6}]\text{Cl}_{3}$ is:
questions.solution:
Ammonia is neutral and the three chlorides are outside the sphere, so the complex ion is $3+$:

$x + 0 = +3 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+3}$.

**Geometrical (cis-trans)** isomerism, since it is square planar.

The **cis** isomer is the anticancer drug cisplatin; the **trans** isomer is inactive. Same atoms, same bonds, different medicine — because only the cis form can bind to two adjacent bases of DNA.

The longest chain is three carbons (propane), with a methyl and a bromine both on C2: **2-bromo-2-methylpropane**.

It is a tertiary halide, and so hydrolyses by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.

questions.q: Tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo hydrolysis predominantly by:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{\text{S}_{\text{N}}1}$ — the tertiary carbocation is well stabilised by three electron-releasing alkyl groups, and the crowded carbon blocks backside attack.

The rate depends only on the halide's concentration, and the product is racemic.

questions.q: HBr adds to propene to give mainly:
questions.solution:
**2-bromopropane** — the reaction goes through the more stable **secondary** carbocation.

In the presence of peroxides the addition is anti-Markovnikov, because the mechanism changes to free radical addition.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl}$ and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ to give:
questions.solution:
**Friedel-Crafts alkylation**, giving toluene.

The $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ generates the electrophile $\text{CH}_{3}^{+}$, and the reaction is **substitution**, which preserves the delocalised ring.

questions.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
questions.solution:
The phenoxide's negative charge is **delocalised into the ring**, which stabilises it. Ethoxide has no such escape route.

$\text{p}K_{a}$: phenol $10$, ethanol $16$ — a factor of a million.
options: the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance

questions.q: Which compound gives a positive Tollens test but a negative iodoform test?
questions.solution:
**Propanal** is an aldehyde, so Tollens' gives a silver mirror — but it has no $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ group, so no iodoform.

Ethanal gives **both**; propanone gives iodoform only; ethanol gives iodoform only.

**Fluoroethanoic acid.** Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so it withdraws electron density most strongly and stabilises the carboxylate best.

The order follows electronegativity: F $>$ Cl $>$ Br $>$ I $>$ H.

questions.q: In aqueous solution, the order of basicity of methylamines is:
questions.solution:
The famous irregular order in **water**: $\mathbf{2° > 1° > 3°}$.

Three effects compete — the inductive effect (favouring $3°$), steric hindrance and **solvation** of the cation through its N–H bonds (both favouring fewer alkyl groups). In the **gas phase**, with no solvent, the order is the simple $3° > 2° > 1°$.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-reducing sugar?
questions.solution:
**Sucrose.** Its glycosidic link joins both anomeric carbons, so neither ring can open to a carbonyl.

Maltose and lactose keep one free anomeric carbon and are reducing. Fructose, though a ketose, is reducing too, because in alkali it isomerises to an aldose.
